analysis.title: Where Will The Fed Funds Peak?
key_insights: Consensus assumes the Fed's terminal rate will settle below the 2023-24 peak. Market pricing has a terminal rate of 4.5-4.75% versus 5.25-5.50% then. TS Lombard argues this view may be too dovish and frames its case as a scenario, not a forecast.

TS Lombard says the consensus rests on three beliefs: the Fed is mostly responding to higher energy prices, the labour market has cooled and proves policy has been restrictive, and 2023-24 rates were 'emergency levels' that will not be seen again.

TS Lombard's official forecast is one 25bps Fed hike per quarter until something 'breaks', which it does not expect before the AI investment boom ends (early 2028?). It says market pricing has moved closer to its view since the start of the year.

Policy may be less restrictive than assumed. The post-COVID fall in inflation and labour market rebalancing may have reflected transitory inflation and supply catch-up rather than demand destruction. That would explain why the economy has been resilient and inflation has settled above target.

The claim that higher rates are stimulative through income transfers to creditors is rejected, because borrowers have higher marginal propensities to consume. A softer version is accepted: effects such as the drag on housing and construction are front-loaded and fade, and nominal income growth has kept the private debt-servicing ratio low.
Fed estimates of r* tend to follow the actual policy rate, so r* is a poor guide to the stance of policy.

The pace of tightening matters. The next wave of hikes is expected to be much more gradual than the 75bps hikes of 2022-23, so the sentiment hit is smaller and the economy has more time to adjust. That makes a higher terminal rate plausible.

The Fed's 'plausible deniability' on its inflation target is gone. Inflation has been above target for 66 months and recently has moved the wrong way, employment is picking up, and new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has criticised his predecessor and reaffirmed the 2% target. TS Lombard concludes the Fed will need to keep hiking until the target is in sight.
The terminal Fed funds rate could end up as high as in 2023-24, or higher, particularly if the AI capex boom continues. TS Lombard's working assumption is that it will.

The path depends on the labour market. TS Lombard says the recovery since the acute policy uncertainty of 2025 faded should continue into 2027, and reduced immigration will bring capacity pressures back.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Market pricing sits below the 5.25-5.50% peak of 2023-24. TS Lombard thinks this is too dovish.
Reference level the consensus expects the Fed not to reach again. TS Lombard says it could be matched or exceeded.
Continued gradual tightening until something breaks.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Removes the Fed's plausible deniability that inflation is returning to target on its own.

risk_factors: The AI investment boom ends sooner than expected, which is what TS Lombard says would 'break' something and end the hiking cycle.
Investors argue the Fed will stop once energy prices come down.
Investors argue growth would crumble if policy returned to its 2024 level.
The labour market recovery stalls before 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: Consensus (the dovish side) says the hiking cycle is a mid-course correction. Energy-driven inflation fades, the labour market has cooled, and terminal rate stays near 4.5-4.75%, below the 2023-24 peak.
tension_points.bear_case: TS Lombard says policy is less restrictive than assumed, the economy is adapting to higher rates, gradual hikes allow a higher terminal rate, and Warsh's stated commitment to 2% removes the Fed's room to tolerate higher inflation. The terminal rate could match or exceed 5.25-5.50%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The AI investment boom ending, which TS Lombard says would 'break' something, or the labour market recovery failing to continue into 2027.
